source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/MayoSmith_1997_WithdrawalPharmacologyMA.pdf, JAMA 1997;278:144–151 (scanned; 8 pages). The machine-read text was used only to find my way. All 8 pages were viewed rendered at 110 dpi. Pp. 144–149 were rendered at 300 dpi, and the abstract, Tables 2, 3 and 4, the Results paragraphs on pp. 145–147 and the working-group list on p. 149 were read on those renders; Table 2 was also checked at 600 dpi. Every number used below was checked on a rendered page. The reference list (pp. 149–151) was read in the machine text and spot-checked on the renders. I re-ran the pooled risk differences from the table counts (DerSimonian–Laird) as a check. Table 5 (regimens) was not recorded.

claims.overstatement: Slight, in 'four small trials': three are small (30, 24 and 15 per arm or fewer), but Kaim et al. (1969) has 103 and 130 patients in the two arms. It supplies 130 of the 186 placebo patients and 8 of the 11 cases, so 'about 6 in 100' mostly reflects one 1969 trial. 'Pooled in a 1997 review' is accurate only in the sense that the review pooled risk differences from these trials. It gives no pooled placebo rate; the 11 of 186 is the editors' sum, which the claim says.
claims.note: Numbers checked on the 300/600-dpi render of Table 2 (p. 145): placebo groups with delirium 2/30 (Rosenfeld and Bizzoco 1961), 1/11 (Sereny and Kalant 1965), 8/130 (Kaim et al. 1969), 0/15 (Zilm et al. 1980). The two 1983 trials did not report delirium. My recomputation of the editors' sum gives the same result: 2+1+8+0 = 11 and 30+11+130+15 = 186, so 11/186 = 5.9%. 'The trials' definitions predate DSM-IV' is true by date (1961–1980 against DSM-IV in 1994). But the review states that it abstracted only trials whose end points corresponded to the DSM-IV definitions (abstract and Methods › Outcomes, pp. 144–145), without saying how that was judged. Suggested wording: the trials predate DSM-IV, and the review does not say how their definitions were matched to it. 'Does not describe their settings' is correct: no setting, population or severity is given for any trial. The guideline also states that it does not cover patients who already have delirium or have had a seizure (p. 144). The review independently supports parts of the predictor list the claim takes from Schuckit (2014): high withdrawal-scale scores predict seizures and delirium (p. 146), and a history of withdrawal seizures is a strong risk factor for seizures (p. 146). Concurrent sedative-hypnotic misuse is a risk factor for major complications, and CIWA-Ar above 15 carries a significant risk of major complications if untreated, which the review labels level I evidence (p. 148). Funding and interests: there is no funding or conflict statement (correct in the claim). One working-group member is listed at the Department of Clinical Pharmacology, Bayer Corporation (p. 149); the claim could say so.

anchors.locator: Abstract (Data Sources, Data Abstraction); Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 144); Methods › Outcomes (pp. 144–145)
anchors.extracted: English-language MEDLINE search to June 1995. The review abstracted only prospective controlled trials whose end points it judged to correspond to the DSM-IV definitions of withdrawal delirium and seizures; how the older trials' definitions were matched is not described. The guideline does not address patients seen after a withdrawal seizure or already in withdrawal delirium, or the choice of inpatient or outpatient setting.

anchors.locator: Results › Structured Assessment Scales and Determination of Dosage, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 146); Results › Special Populations, 2nd paragraph, and Recommendations › Determination of Dose, consideration 1 (p. 148)
anchors.extracted: High withdrawal-scale scores predict the development of seizures and delirium (refs 69, 107). A history of withdrawal seizures is a strong risk factor for seizures in a withdrawal episode. Concurrent sedative-hypnotic misuse has been identified as a risk factor for major complications. Severe withdrawal (CIWA-Ar above 15) carries a significant risk of major complications if untreated (labelled level I evidence). This corroborates the predictor list the claim cites to Schuckit (2014).

claims.overstatement: Mild, for the editor. 'Benzodiazepines compared with placebo reduced withdrawal seizures' is causal while the claim's certainty is low; GRADE-style wording at low certainty would be 'may reduce'. In this review the placebo-controlled trials are called prospective, not randomized; the claim's parenthesis rests the randomization on the Cochrane review. The phenothiazine sentences are worded as associations ('were followed by'), which fits.
claims.note: All Mayo-Smith numbers in the statement and magnitude were checked on the rendered pages and match. Table 2 (p. 145): delirium −4.9 per 100 (−9.0 to −0.7), P = .04, 4 trials; seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), 5 trials. The seizure P value is printed as < .001 in Table 2 but .003 in the abstract (p. 144) and the Results text (p. 145); the claim gives no P value. Table 4 (p. 147): phenothiazine against placebo, delirium 0.0 (−5.8 to +6.6) and seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9); against benzodiazepine or paraldehyde, delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8) and seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6). The claim correctly uses the table's 11.4, not the 12.4 printed in the Results text on p. 147. It also does not repeat the text's statement that phenothiazines increase seizures compared with placebo, which Table 4 does not show. I recomputed the editors' sums from Table 2 and got the same: delirium, benzodiazepine 2+0+1+0 = 3 of 30+24+103+15 = 172, against placebo 11 of 186; seizures, 0+1+0+0+0 = 1 of 24+103+15+25+15 = 182, against 0+9+2+4+2 = 17 of 11+130+15+25+15 = 196. Trial years 1961 to 1983 and 'most of them of chlordiazepoxide' (4 of the 6) are correct. 'One trial from 1969 supplies most of the events' is correct: Kaim et al. have 9 of the 14 delirium events and 10 of the 18 seizure events in Table 2. They also dominate the phenothiazine comparisons (chlorpromazine 7/98 and 12/98 against chlordiazepoxide 1/103 and 1/103). 'The two reviews share three trials' cannot be checked from this source alone; Table 2's six trials are Rosenfeld and Bizzoco 1961, Sereny and Kalant 1965, Kaim et al. 1969, Zilm et al. 1980, Sellers et al. 1983 and Naranjo et al. 1983. On 'outcome definitions predate DSM-IV', see the note on cl_alc_withdrawal_delirium: the review says it kept only end points corresponding to DSM-IV, without saying how. Robustness, from my own recalculation: the printed −4.9 and −7.7 are reproduced exactly by random-effects pooling of risk differences without a continuity correction. Under that method the trials with no events in either arm (Zilm et al. for delirium; Sereny and Kalant for seizures) carry no weight, so the estimates rest effectively on 3 and 4 trials. With 0.5 added to zero cells for the variance, the estimates are −4.3 (−8.2 to −0.3) and −6.7 (−10.7 to −2.6): same direction, and both still exclude zero. The claim's 'people with serious ... disease or other drug dependence were usually left out' is consistent with p. 148: no studies were found reporting management in people with specific coexisting medical or substance use disorders. On the pooled comparison with other medicines (taken from Amato et al.), this review adds a consistent qualifier: beta-blockers, clonidine and carbamazepine ease withdrawal severity, but the evidence was inadequate to judge their effect on delirium or seizures (abstract, p. 144; pp. 146–147). The claim contains no dose or regimen.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Summary and meta-analysis row; Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 1st paragraph; Methods › Review of the Evidence (random-effects model, risk differences)
anchors.extracted: Benzodiazepine against placebo, random-effects risk differences: delirium −4.9 cases per 100 patients (95% CI −9.0 to −0.7), P = .04, from 4 trials with delirium data (benzodiazepine 3/172, placebo 11/186, editors' sums recomputed); seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), P < .001 in the table (P = .003 in the abstract and text), from 5 trials (1/182 against 17/196, editors' sums recomputed). Trials 1961–1983; chlordiazepoxide in 4, diazepam and lorazepam in 1 each.

anchors.locator: Table 4 (Prospective, controlled trials of neuroleptic agents), Summary and meta-analysis rows; Results › Neuroleptic Agents
anchors.extracted: Phenothiazine (promazine, chlorpromazine) against placebo (2 trials: Sereny and Kalant 1965; Kaim et al. 1969): delirium 0.0 per 100 (−5.8 to +6.6), P = .92; seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9), P = .19. Against cross-tolerant medication (benzodiazepine or paraldehyde; Thomas and Freedman 1964, Sereny and Kalant, Chambers and Schultz 1965, Kaim et al.): delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8), P = .002; seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6), P < .001. The Results text gives 12.4 for the seizure difference and says these agents increase seizures compared with placebo, which the table's interval does not show.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Kaim et al. (1969) rows and Rosenfeld and Bizzoco (1961) rows
anchors.extracted: One trial dominates: Kaim et al. 1969, chlordiazepoxide 1/103 against placebo 8/130 for delirium (RR 0.16, 0.02 to 1.24, P = .08) and 1/103 against 9/130 for seizures (RR 0.14, 0.02 to 1.09, P = .046), i.e. 9 of 14 delirium events and 10 of 18 seizure events in the table. Rosenfeld and Bizzoco 1961 found 2/30 against 2/30 for delirium. Recalculation from these counts: the printed pooled estimates are reproduced only without a continuity correction; with 0.5 added to zero cells for the variance they are −4.3 (−8.2 to −0.3) and −6.7 (−10.7 to −2.6) per 100.

anchors.locator: Abstract, Data Synthesis (p. 144); Results › Other Agents and Special Populations, 2nd paragraph (p. 148)
anchors.extracted: Beta-blockers, clonidine and carbamazepine ease withdrawal severity, but the evidence is inadequate to determine their effect on delirium and seizures; no other agent has been shown to reduce delirium or seizures. No studies were identified on managing withdrawal in people with specific coexisting medical or substance use disorders, in adolescents, in older people or in pregnancy.

key_findings.correction: The 'about 10% of US detoxification programmes' refers to barbiturates in general, not to phenobarbital: the review says barbiturates are used by about 10% of US detoxification programmes (ref 6), and then that no controlled trials of phenobarbital could be identified (p. 146, Results › Benzodiazepines and Other Sedative-Hypnotic Agents, 5th paragraph). The rest of the finding is confirmed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the core conclusion fits the pooled data; the five listed gaps are real.

missed: How the pooled risk differences were computed. The printed Table 2 estimates (delirium −4.9, −9.0 to −0.7; seizures −7.7, −12.0 to −3.5) and Table 4's +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6) are reproduced exactly by DerSimonian–Laird pooling without any continuity correction (editors' recalculation). Under that method, trials with no events in either arm carry no weight (Zilm et al. 1980 for delirium; Sereny and Kalant 1965 for seizures), so the estimates rest effectively on 3 and 4 trials. Arms with zero events also contribute no variance, which over-weights them. With 0.5 added to zero cells for the variance, the Table 2 estimates are −4.3 (−8.2 to −0.3) and −6.7 (−10.7 to −2.6): same direction, both still excluding zero.

Table 4, phenothiazine against placebo: the printed delirium estimate 0.0 is not the midpoint of its own interval (−5.8 to +6.6, midpoint +0.4); recalculation gives +0.4 (−5.8 to +6.6). The seizure estimate +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9) is not reproduced from the counts: +5.9 (−1.1 to +13.0) with a continuity correction, +6.4 (−0.1 to +12.9) without. Every method gives an interval that includes zero, so reporting issue 2 stands. Minor.
